'''Francis Sellers Collins''' {{postnominals|list=[[Foreign Member of the Royal Society|ForMemRS]]}} (born April 15, 1950) is an American [[physician-scientist]] who discovered the genes associated with a number of diseases and led the [[Human Genome Project]]. He served as director of the [[National Institutes of Health]] (NIH) in [[Bethesda, Maryland]], from 17 August 2009 to 19 December 2021, serving under three presidents.<ref name="hhs"/><ref name="WaPo" /> Collins announced his retirement publicly from the NIH on March 1, 2025, after 32 years of service.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Stein |first=Rob |date=2025-03-01 |title=Legendary former NIH director retires from embattled agency |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/shots-health-news/2025/03/01/g-s1-51514/francis-collins-nih-national-institutes-health-resigns |access-date=2025-03-01 |work=NPR |language=en}}</ref>

Before being appointed director of the NIH, Collins led the Human Genome Project and other genomics research initiatives as director of the [[National Human Genome Research Institute]] (NHGRI), one of the 27 institutes and centers at NIH. Before joining NHGRI, he earned a reputation as a gene hunter at the [[University of Michigan]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1990/09/21/gene-therapy-cures-cystic-fibrosis-in-lab/|title=Gene Therapy Cures Cystic Fibrosis In Lab|work=tribunedigital-chicagotribune|access-date=January 5, 2018}}</ref> He has been elected to the [[Institute of Medicine]] and the [[National Academy of Sciences]], and has received the [[Presidential Medal of Freedom]] and the [[National Medal of Science]].

Collins has written books on science, medicine, and religion, including the ''[[New York Times]]'' bestseller ''[[The Language of God: A Scientist Presents Evidence for Belief]]''. After leaving the directorship of NHGRI and before becoming director of the NIH, he founded and served as president of [[The BioLogos Foundation]], which promotes discourse on the [[relationship between science and religion]] and advocates the perspective that belief in Christianity can be reconciled with acceptance of evolution and science, especially through the [[theistic evolution]] idea that the Creator brought about his plan through the processes of evolution.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://biologos.org/about |title=About The BioLogos Foundation |publisher=The Biologos Foundation |access-date=May 3, 2014 |quote=We embrace the historical Christian faith, upholding the authority and inspiration of the Bible. We affirm evolutionary creation, recognizing God as Creator of all life over billions of years. We seek truth, ever learning as we study the natural world and the Bible. |archive-date=August 29, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110829121912/http://biologos.org/about }}</ref> In 2009, [[Pope Benedict XVI]] appointed Collins to the [[Pontifical Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.ewtnnews.com/vatican/human-genome-and-embryology-experts-named-to-pontifical-academy-of-sciences|title=Human genome and embryology experts named to Pontifical Academy of Sciences|work=Catholic News Agency|access-date=January 5, 2018}}</ref>

On October 5, 2021, Collins announced that he would resign as NIH director by the end of the year.<ref name="resignation"/> Four months later in February 2022, he joined the [[Cabinet of Joe Biden]] as Acting [[Science Advisor to the President]], replacing [[Eric Lander]].<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.newyorker.com/news/persons-of-interest/faith-science-and-francis-collins|title=Faith, Science and Francis Collins|magazine=[[The New Yorker]]|date=April 7, 2022|access-date=May 5, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://usun.usmission.gov/keynote-remarks-at-the-7th-multi-stakeholder-forum-on-science-technology-and-innovation-for-the-sdgs-sti-forum/|title=Keynote Remarks at the 7th Multi-stakeholder Forum on Science, Technology, and Innovation for the SDGs (STI Forum)|date=May 5, 2022 |publisher=United States Mission to the United Nations|access-date=May 5, 2022}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Francis Sellers Collins was born in [[Staunton, Virginia]], the youngest of four sons of Fletcher Collins and Margaret James Collins. Raised on a small farm in Virginia's [[Shenandoah Valley]], Collins was [[home schooled]]  until the sixth grade.<ref>Collins, Francis. ''[[The Language of God: A Scientist Presents Evidence for Belief]]''. [https://books.google.com/books?id=JcMCmBnpHGsC&dq=%22language+of+god%22+collins+homeschool&pg=PA13 Chapter 1].</ref> He attended [[Robert E. Lee High School (Staunton, Virginia)|Robert E. Lee High School]] in Staunton, Virginia. Through most of his high school and college years he aspired to be a chemist, and he had little interest in what he then considered the "messy" field of [[biology]]. What he referred to as his "formative education" was received at the [[University of Virginia]], where he earned a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in [[chemistry]] in 1970. He went on to graduate as a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in [[physical chemistry]] at [[Yale University]] in 1974.<ref name="thesis-collins-1974">{{cite thesis |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/288233821/ |title=Semiclassical theory of vibrationally inelastic-scattering, with application to proton + hydrogen molecule. |date=1974 |publisher=[[Yale University]] |type=Ph.D. |last=Collins |first=Francis Sellers |id={{ProQuest|288233821}} |url-access=limited |oclc=702791906}}</ref>

During his time at Yale, a course in [[biochemistry]] sparked his interest in the subject. After consulting with his mentor from the University of Virginia, Carl Trindle, he changed fields and enrolled in medical school at the [[UNC School of Medicine|University of North Carolina School of Medicine]], earning a [[Doctor of Medicine]] degree there in 1977.<ref>{{Cite web|title=225 Years of Tar Heels: Francis Collins {{!}} UNC-Chapel Hill|url=https://www.unc.edu/posts/2019/03/25/225-years-of-tar-heels-francis-collins/|date=2019-03-25|website=The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill|language=en-US|access-date=2020-05-11}}</ref> From 1978 to 1981, Collins served a [[Residency (medicine)|residency]] and chief residency in internal medicine at [[North Carolina Memorial Hospital]] in [[Chapel Hill, North Carolina|Chapel Hill]]. He then returned to Yale, where he was a [[fellow]] in human genetics at the medical school from 1980 to 1983.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Francis S. Collins, M.D., Ph.D.|url=https://www.genome.gov/10001018/former-nhgri-director-francis-collins-biography|access-date=2021-10-12|website=Genome.gov|language=en}}</ref>

==Genetics research==
At Yale, Collins worked under the direction of [[Sherman Weissman]], and in 1984 the two published a paper, "Directional cloning of DNA fragments at a large distance from an initial probe: a circularization method".<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Francis S. Collins |author2=Sherman M. Weissman |title=''Directional cloning of DNA fragments at a large distance from an initial probe: a circularization method'' |publisher=Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA |date=Nov 1984 |doi=10.1073/pnas.81.21.6812 |pmid=6093122 |pmc=392022 |volume=81 |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |issue=21 |pages=6812–6816|bibcode=1984PNAS...81.6812C |doi-access=free }}</ref> The method described was named ''[[chromosome jumping]]'', to emphasize the contrast with an older and much more time-consuming method of copying DNA fragments called ''[[chromosome walking]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Leon. E. Rosenberg |author-link=Leon E. Rosenberg |title=''Introductory Speech for Francis S. Collins'' |year=2006 |pmc=1559551 |pmid=16909377 |doi=10.1086/500276 |volume=79 |issue=3 |journal=Am J Hum Genet |pages=419–20}}</ref> Collins joined the [[University of Michigan]] faculty in 1984, rising to the rank of professor in internal medicine and human genetics.  His gene-hunting approach, which he named "[[positional cloning]]",<ref>{{cite web |url=https://rowan.biology.ualberta.ca/courses/genet302/uploads/winter11/gane/private/genet302-GW-week3_noQ.pdf |title=Positional cloning of human disease genes: a reversal of scientific priorities |publisher=University of Alberta, Department of Biological Science |access-date=October 16, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120425021226/https://rowan.biology.ualberta.ca/courses/genet302/uploads/winter11/gane/private/genet302-GW-week3_noQ.pdf |archive-date=April 25, 2012 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=Collins F |s2cid=30491698 |year=1992 |title=Positional Cloning: Let's not call it reverse anymore |journal=Nature Genetics |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=3–6 |doi=10.1038/ng0492-3 |pmid=1301996}}</ref> developed into a powerful component of modern molecular genetics.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Positional cloning reaches maturity |last=Nelson |first=David L. |date=Jun 1995 |journal=Curr Opin Genet Dev |doi=10.1016/0959-437X(95)80042-5 |pmid=7549422 |volume=5 |issue=3 |pages=298–303}}</ref>

Several scientific teams worked in the 1970s and 1980s to identify genes and their loci as a cause of [[cystic fibrosis]]. Progress was modest until 1985, when [[Lap-Chee Tsui]] and colleagues at Toronto's Hospital for Sick Children identified the locus for the gene.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Tsui |first=LC |author2=Buchwald M |author3=Barker D |title=Cystic fibrosis locus defined by a genetically linked polymorphic DNA marker |journal=Science |date=November 29, 1985 |volume=230 |issue=4729 |pages=1054–1057 |doi=10.1126/science.2997931 |pmid=2997931 |bibcode = 1985Sci...230.1054T }}<!--|access-date=May 9, 2014--></ref>  It was then determined that a shortcut was needed to speed the process of identification, so Tsui contacted Collins, who agreed to collaborate with the Toronto team and share his chromosome-jumping technique. The gene was identified in June 1989,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hhmi.org/genetictrail/a120.html |title=''Blazing a Genetic Trail/.../Jumping Toward the Gene'' |author=Pines, Maya |publisher=Howard Hughes Medical Institute |year=2008 |access-date=October 16, 2011 |archive-date=March 17, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180317102345/http://www.hhmi.org/blazing-a-genetic-trail }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hhmi.org/genetictrail/a130.html |title=''Stalking a Lethal Gene:Discovering the Gene for Cystic Fibrosis'' |author=Pines, Maya |publisher=Howard Hughes Medical Institute |year=2008 |access-date=October 16, 2011 |archive-date=March 17, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180317102345/http://www.hhmi.org/blazing-a-genetic-trail }}</ref> and the results were published in the journal ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' on September 8, 1989.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Marx |first1=J. |year=1989 |title=The cystic fibrosis gene is found |journal=Science |volume=245 |issue=4921 |pages=923–5 |bibcode=1989Sci...245..923M |doi=10.1126/science.2772644 |pmid=2772644}}</ref> This identification was followed by other genetic discoveries made by Collins and a variety of collaborators. They included isolation of the genes for [[Huntington's disease]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=MacDonald |first1=M |s2cid=802885 |year=1993 |title=A novel gene containing a trinucleotide repeat that is expanded and unstable on Huntington's disease chromosomes |journal=Cell |volume=72 |issue=6 |pages=971–83 |doi=10.1016/0092-8674(93)90585-E |pmid=8458085|hdl=2027.42/30901 |url=https://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/bitstream/2027.42/30901/3/0000570.pdf |hdl-access=free}}</ref> [[neurofibromatosis]],<ref>{{cite book |title=Rubin's Pathology: Clinicopathologic Foundation of Medicine |first1=Raphael |last1=Rubin |first2=David S. |last2=Strayer |publisher=Wolters Kluwer Health: Lippincott Williams & Wilkins |edition=5th |date=2008 |location=Baltimore |pages=201–03 |isbn=978-0-7817-9516-6}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author=Fauci|title=Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine (Small textbook) |edition=16th |page=2453|display-authors=etal}}</ref> [[multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chandrasekharappa |first1=S. C. |last2=Guru |first2=S. C. |last3=Manickam |first3=P |last4=Olufemi |first4=S. E. |last5=Collins |first5=F. S. |last6=Emmert-Buck |first6=M. R. |last7=Debelenko |first7=L. V. |last8=Zhuang |first8=Z |last9=Lubensky |first9=I. A. |last10=Liotta |first10=L. A. |last11=Crabtree |first11=J. S. |last12=Wang |first12=Y |last13=Roe |first13=B. A. |last14=Weisemann |first14=J |last15=Boguski|author-link15= Mark Boguski|first15=M. S. |last16=Agarwal |first16=S. K. |last17=Kester |first17=M. B. |last18=Kim |first18=Y. S. |last19=Heppner |first19=C |last20=Dong |first20=Q |last21=Spiegel |first21=A. M. |last22=Burns |first22=A. L. |last23=Marx |first23=S. J. |year=1997 |title=Positional Cloning of the Gene for Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia-Type 1 |journal=Science |volume=276 |issue=5311 |pages=404–07 |doi=10.1126/science.276.5311.404 |pmid=9103196|url=https://zenodo.org/record/1231108 }}</ref> inv(16) AML<ref>Science 261 (5124): 1041–4</ref> and [[Hutchinson–Gilford progeria syndrome]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Eriksson |first1=Maria |last2=Brown |first2=W. Ted |last3=Gordon |first3=Leslie B. |last4=Glynn |first4=Michael W. |last5=Singer |first5=Joel |last6=Scott |first6=Laura |last7=Erdos |first7=Michael R. |last8=Robbins |first8=Christiane M. |last9=Moses |first9=Tracy Y. |last10=Berglund |first10=Peter |last11=Dutra |first11=Amalia |last12=Pak |first12=Evgenia |last13=Durkin |first13=Sandra |last14=Csoka |first14=Antonei B. |last15=Boehnke |first15=Michael |last16=Glover |first16=Thomas W. |last17=Collins |first17=Francis S. |s2cid=4420150 |year=2003 |title=Recurrent de novo point mutations in lamin a cause Hutchinson–Gilford progeria syndrome |journal=Nature |volume=423 |issue=6937 |pages=293–98 |bibcode=2003Natur.423..293E |doi=10.1038/nature01629 |pmid=12714972|pmc=10540076 |hdl=2027.42/62684 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==Genomics==
In 1992, National Institutes of Health Director [[Bernadine Healy]] appointed Collins to succeed [[James D. Watson]] as director of the [[Human Genome Project|National Center for Human Genome Research]], which became [[National Human Genome Research Institute]] (NHGRI) in 1997. As director he oversaw the International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.genome.gov/11006939|title=IHG Sequencing Centers|website=National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI)|access-date=March 29, 2018}}</ref> which was the group that successfully carried out the [[Human Genome Project]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Francis S. Collins, M.D., Ph.D. Biography and Interview |website=www.achievement.org|publisher=[[American Academy of Achievement]]|url= https://www.achievement.org/achiever/francis-s-collins/#interview}}</ref> In 1994, Collins founded NHGRI's Division of Intramural Research, a collection of investigator-directed laboratories that conduct genome research on the NIH campus.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.genome.gov/10001036 |title=The Division of Intramural Research |editor=National Human Genome Research Institute |access-date=October 16, 2011}}</ref>

In June 2000 Collins was joined by President Bill Clinton and biologist [[Craig Venter]] in making the announcement of a working draft of the [[human genome]].<ref>Jamie Shreeve, "[https://www.usnews.com/usnews/news/articles/051031/31genome.htm The Blueprint of Life] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071130184339/http://www.usnews.com/usnews/news/articles/051031/31genome.htm |date=November 30, 2007 }}," ''[[U.S. News & World Report]]'', 10/31/05, URL accessed January 30, 2007.</ref> He stated that "It is humbling for me, and awe-inspiring to realize that we have caught the first glimpse of our own instruction book, previously known only to God."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://articles.latimes.com/2006/aug/17/nation/na-collins17/3 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140503121231/http://articles.latimes.com/2006/aug/17/nation/na-collins17/3 |archive-date=May 3, 2014 |title=Faithful to God, Science |last=Simon |first=Stephanie |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |access-date=May 3, 2014 |quote="It is humbling for me, and awe-inspiring," he said, standing at Clinton's side, "to realize that we have caught the first glimpse of our own instruction book, previously known only to God." That moment moved Collins -- who is married and has two grown daughters — to talk more publicly about his faith and to write the book. "It's been a bit like taking a public bath," he said.}}</ref><ref name="Lennox2009">{{cite book |last=Lennox |first=John C. |title=God's Undertaker: Has Science Buried God? |year=2009 |publisher=Lion Books |isbn=978-0-7459-5371-7 |page=[https://archive.org/details/godsundertaker00john/page/176 176] |quote=At the public announcement of the completion of the Human Genome Project, its director, Francis Collins, said: 'It is humbling for me and awe-inspiring to realize that we have caught the first glimpse of our own instruction book, previously known only to God.' |url=https://archive.org/details/godsundertaker00john/page/176 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://transcripts.cnn.com/TRANSCRIPTS/0006/26/bn.01.html |title=President Clinton, British Prime Minister Tony Blair Deliver Remarks on Human Genome Milestone |date=June 26, 2000 |publisher=[[CNN]] |access-date=May 3, 2014 |archive-date=March 7, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210307193722/http://transcripts.cnn.com/TRANSCRIPTS/0006/26/bn.01.html }}</ref> An initial analysis was published in February 2001, and scientists worked toward finishing the reference version of the human genome sequence by 2003, coinciding with the 50th anniversary of [[James D. Watson]] and [[Francis Crick]]'s publication of the structure of [[DNA]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Research Goals |url=https://doe-humangenomeproject.ornl.gov/u-s-human-genome-project-research-goals/ |website=Human Genome Project |publisher=U.S. Department of Energy |access-date=1 January 2025}}</ref>

Another major activity at NHGRI during his tenure as director was the creation of the [[haplotype map]] of the human genome. This [[International HapMap Project]] produced a catalog of human genetic variations—called [[single-nucleotide polymorphisms]]—which is now being used to discover variants correlated with disease risk. Among the labs engaged in that effort is Collins's own lab at NHGRI, which has sought to identify and understand the genetic variations that influence the risk of developing [[type 2 diabetes]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Francis Collins, M.D., Ph.D. {{!}} Principal Investigators |url=https://irp.nih.gov/pi/francis-collins |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120823182447/http://irp.nih.gov/pi/francis-collins |archive-date=August 23, 2012 |website=NIH Intramural Research Program |publisher=National Institutes of Health |access-date=1 January 2025}}</ref>

In addition to his basic genetic research and scientific leadership, Collins is known for his close attention to ethical and legal issues in genetics. He has been a strong advocate for protecting the privacy of genetic information and has served as a national leader in securing the passage of the federal Genetic Information and Nondiscrimination Act, which prohibits gene-based discrimination in employment and health insurance.<ref name=interview>{{cite web |url=https://www.pbs.org/wnet/religionandethics/transcripts/collins.html |title=Transcript, Bob Abernethy's interview with Dr. Francis Collins, director of the Human Genome Project at the National Institutes of Health. |publisher=PBS, Religion and Ethics Newsweekly |access-date=October 16, 2011 |archive-date=September 10, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110910201923/http://www.pbs.org/wnet/religionandethics/transcripts/collins.html }}</ref> In 2013, spurred by concerns over the publication of the genome of the widely used [[HeLa]] cell line derived from the late [[Henrietta Lacks]], Collins and other NIH leaders worked with the Lacks family to reach an agreement to protect their privacy, while giving researchers controlled access to the genomic data.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nih.gov/about/director/statement-hela-08072013.htm|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130830225004/http://www.nih.gov/about/director/statement-hela-08072013.htm|archive-date=August 30, 2013|title=The HeLa Genome: An Agreement on Privacy and Access |date=June 13, 2016|publisher=[[National Institutes of Health]]|access-date=March 29, 2018}}</ref>

Building on his own experiences as a physician volunteer in a rural missionary hospital in [[Nigeria]],<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/11/30/science/scientist-at-work-francis-s-collins-unlocking-the-secrets-of-the-genome.html?pagewanted=all&src=pm |title=Scientist at work: Francis S. Collins; unlocking the secrets of the Genome |work=[[The New York Times]]|first=Gina|last=Kolate|date=November 30, 1993|access-date=June 24, 2024}}</ref> Collins is also very interested in opening avenues for genome research to benefit the health of people living in developing nations. For example, in 2010, he helped establish an initiative called [[Human Heredity and Health in Africa]] (H3Africa) to advance African capacity and expertise in genomic science.<ref>[http://www.genome.gov/27540084 National Institutes of Health, "NIH and Wellcome Trust Announce Partnership to Support Population-Based Genome Studies in Africa," ''NIH News,'' June 22, 2010]</ref> Collins announced his resignation as NHGRI director on May 28, 2008, but continued to lead an active lab there with a research focus<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://irp.nih.gov/pi/francis-collins|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120823182447/http://irp.nih.gov/pi/francis-collins|archive-date=August 23, 2012|title=Principal Investigators|website=NIH Intramural Research Program|access-date=2019-07-30}}</ref> on progeria and type 2 diabetes<ref>[[Chemical & Engineering News]], Vol. 86 No. 31, August 4, 2008, p. 33, "Francis Collins leaves NIH"</ref> until his resignation on February 28, 2025.

==NIH director==
===Nomination and confirmation===
[[File:Francis Collins with Kathleen Sebelius after swearing-in ceremony.jpg|right|thumb|Collins with Health and Human Services Secretary [[Kathleen Sebelius]] after swearing-in ceremony]]
On July 8, 2009, President Barack Obama nominated Collins as director of the National Institutes of Health,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the_press_office/President-Obama-Announces-Intent-to-Nominate-Francis-Collins-as-NIH-Director/|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title="President Obama Announces Intent to Nominate Francis Collins as NIH Director," Press Office, the White House, July 8, 2009|date=July 8, 2009|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|access-date=March 29, 2018}}</ref> and the Senate unanimously confirmed him for the post. He was sworn in by Health and Human Services Secretary [[Kathleen Sebelius]] on August 17, 2009.<ref name="hhs">[https://www.hhs.gov/news/press/2009pres/08/20090807d.html Secretary Sebelius Announces Senate Confirmation of Dr. Francis Collins as Director of the National Institutes of Health] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120921064420/http://www.hhs.gov/news/press/2009pres/08/20090807d.html |date=September 21, 2012 }} 7-Aug-09</ref> ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' writer Jocelyn Kaiser opined that Collins was "known as a skilled administrator and excellent communicator", that Obama's nomination "did not come as a big surprise", and that the appointment "ignited a volley of flattering remarks from researchers and biomedical groups." She also wrote that Collins "does have his critics", some of them who were concerned with the new director's "outspoken Christian faith".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kaiser |first1=J. |year=2009 |title=White House Taps Former Genome Chief Francis Collins as NIH Director |journal=Science |volume=325 |issue=5938 |pages=250–51 |pmid=19608881 |doi=10.1126/science.325_250a}}</ref> ''[[Washington Post]]'' staffer David Brown wrote that Collins's status as a "[[born-again Christian]] ... may help him build bridges with those who view some gene-based research as a potential threat to religious values."<ref name="wp">{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/07/08/AR2009070802769.html |title=Obama picks Francis Collins as new NIH Director |newspaper=Washington Post |date=July 8, 2009 |access-date=October 16, 2011}}</ref> Collins's appointment was welcomed by the [[chief executive officer]] of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]],<ref name="wp" /> and by [[Bernadine Healy]], the former head of the [[National Institutes of Health]].<ref>[http://health.usnews.com/blogs/heart-to-heart/2009/07/09/francis-collins-leader-for-the-21st-century-nih.html Francis Collins Leader for the 21st Century NIH] [[U.S. News & World Report]] 9-June-09</ref>

In October 2009, shortly after his appointment as NIH director, Collins stated in an interview in ''[[The New York Times]]'': "I have made it clear that I have no religious agenda for the N.I.H., and I think the vast majority of scientists have been reassured by that and have moved on."<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/10/06/health/06nih.html |work=The New York Times |title=For N.I.H. Chief, Issues of Identity and Culture |first=Gardiner |last=Harris |date=October 6, 2009 |access-date=May 2, 2010}}</ref> On October 1, 2009, in the second of his four appearances on ''[[The Colbert Report]]'', Collins discussed his leadership at the NIH and other topics such as [[personalized medicine]] and [[stem cell research]]. And, in November 2011, Collins was included on ''The New Republic's'' list of Washington's most powerful, least famous people.  Collins appeared on the series finale of ''The Colbert Report'', participating in a [[Choir|chorus]] with several other famous people singing "[[We'll Meet Again]]".<ref>{{cite magazine  |title=Washington's Most Powerful, Least Famous People |url=http://www.tnr.com/article/politics/96131/washingtons-most-powerful-least-famous-people?passthru=ZTM3Y2VhYmZjNmIzMjllNzQ3MjMxOGEzMmJlZjg1NzI |magazine=The New Republic |date=November 3, 2011 |access-date=October 25, 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.colbertnation.com/the-colbert-report-videos/250628/october-01-2009/francis-collins |title=Francis Collins |date=October 1, 2009 |access-date=October 18, 2009 |publisher=[[The Colbert Report]]}}</ref>

On June 6, 2017, President [[Donald Trump]] announced his selection of Collins to continue to serve as the NIH Director.<ref>{{cite web |title=Collins Will Stay On at NIH |url=https://www.insidehighered.com/news/2017/06/07/president-trump-keeps-francis-collins-head-nih |website=Inside Higher Ed |date=June 7, 2017 |access-date=16 February 2022}}</ref> On 19 December 2017, Collins and the NIH lifted the Obama moratorium on [[Gain-of-function research|gain of function research]] because it was deemed to be "important in helping us identify, understand, and develop strategies and effective countermeasures against rapidly evolving pathogens that pose a threat to [[public health]]."<ref name="nihd19">{{cite news |last1=Collins |first1=Francis S. |title=NIH Lifts Funding Pause on Gain-of-Function Research |url=https://www.nih.gov/about-nih/who-we-are/nih-director/statements/nih-lifts-funding-pause-gain-function-research |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171222223351/https://www.nih.gov/about-nih/who-we-are/nih-director/statements/nih-lifts-funding-pause-gain-function-research |archive-date=December 22, 2017 |publisher=Director, National Institutes of Health |date=19 December 2017}}</ref> In October 2020, Collins criticized the [[Great Barrington Declaration]]'s "focused protection" herd immunity strategy, calling it "a fringe component of epidemiology. This is not mainstream science. It's dangerous. It fits into the political views of certain parts of our confused political establishment."<ref name="BostonGlobe">{{cite news |last=Finucane |first=Martin |date=14 October 2020 |title=Boston Researchers Join Letter in The Lancet Rejecting Herd Immunity Strategy |newspaper=The Boston Globe |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2020/10/14/nation/boston-researchers-join-letter-lancet-rejecting-herd-immunity-strategy/ |access-date=18 October 2020 |url-access = subscription}}</ref> In a private email to Fauci, Collins called the authors of the declaration "fringe epidemiologists" and said: "There needs to be a quick and devastating published take down of its premises."<ref name=":102">{{Cite web |last=Gillespie |first=Nick |date=2022-04-20 |title=Dr. Jay Bhattacharya: How To Avoid 'Absolutely Catastrophic' COVID Mistakes |url=https://reason.com/podcast/2022/04/20/dr-jay-bhattacharya-how-to-avoid-absolutely-catastrophic-covid-mistakes/ |access-date=2022-04-21 |website=[[Reason.com]] |language=en-US|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251205102125/https://reason.com/podcast/2022/04/20/dr-jay-bhattacharya-how-to-avoid-absolutely-catastrophic-covid-mistakes/|archive-date=2025-12-05|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":12">{{Cite news |last= |first= |date=2021-12-21 |title=How Fauci and Collins Shut Down Covid Debate |language=en-US |work=The Wall Street Journal |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/fauci-collins-emails-great-barrington-declaration-covid-pandemic-lockdown-11640129116 |access-date=2022-05-12 |issn=0099-9660|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211222000825/https://www.wsj.com/articles/fauci-collins-emails-great-barrington-declaration-covid-pandemic-lockdown-11640129116|archive-date=2021-12-22|url-status=live}}</ref> ''[[The Wall Street Journal]]''<nowiki/>'s [[editorial board]] accused Collins of "work[ing] with the media to trash the Great Barrington Declaration" and of "Shut[ting] Down Covid Debate".<ref name=":12" /> On January 15, 2021, President-elect [[Joe Biden]] announced his selection of Collins to continue to serve as NIH Director.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-01-15|title=President-elect Biden Announces Key Members of his White House Science Team|url=https://buildbackbetter.gov/press-releases/president-elect-biden-announces-key-members-of-his-white-house-science-team/|access-date=2021-01-15|website=President-Elect Joe Biden|language=en-US|archive-date=January 20, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210120170851/https://buildbackbetter.gov/press-releases/president-elect-biden-announces-key-members-of-his-white-house-science-team/}}</ref> On October 5, 2021, Collins announced that he would resign as NIH director by the end of the year.<ref name="resignation">{{Cite web|date=2021-10-04|title=Francis Collins to step down as director of the National Institutes of Health|url=https://www.nih.gov/news-events/news-releases/francis-collins-step-down-director-national-institutes-health|access-date=2021-10-05|website=National Institutes of Health (NIH)|language=EN|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260416073529/https://www.nih.gov/news-events/news-releases/francis-collins-step-down-director-national-institutes-health|archive-date=2026-04-16|url-status=live}}</ref> His last day was 19 December 2021.<ref name="WaPo">{{cite news |last1=Sellers |first1=Stead |title=Leadership During Crisis with Francis S. Collins, MD, PhD |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/washington-post-live/2021/12/17/leadership-during-crisis-with-francis-s-collins-md-phd/ |newspaper=Washington Post }}</ref>

===Projects===
Collins was instrumental in establishing the [[National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences]] (NCATS) on December 23, 2011.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nih.gov/news/health/dec2011/od-23.htm|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130830225011/http://www.nih.gov/news/health/dec2011/od-23.htm|archive-date=August 30, 2013|title=NIH establishes National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences|date=September 18, 2015|website=nih.gov|access-date=March 29, 2018}}</ref> In January 2013, Collins created two senior scientific positions on [[Big data|Big Data]],<ref>{{Cite report|author1-link=John Sarrao|last=Sarrao|first=John Louis|date=2018-06-04|title=Prepared Statement of Dr. John Sarrao, Principal Associate Director, Science, Technology & Engineering, Los Alamos National Laboratory|doi=10.2172/1440505|osti=1440505|s2cid=115287921}}</ref> as well as the diversity of the scientific workforce.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Valantine|first=Hannah A.|s2cid=22127481|date=November 2017|title=50 Years to Gender Parity: Can STEM Afford to Wait?: A Cardiologist and NIH Chief Officer of Scientific Workforce Diversity Reflects on What It Will Take to Keep Women in Biomedicine|journal=IEEE Pulse|volume=8|issue=6|pages=46–48|doi=10.1109/mpul.2017.2750839|pmid=29155378|issn=2154-2287}}</ref> Other projects he took on early in his tenure included increased support for [[Alzheimer's disease]] research, which was announced in May 2012;<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://nihrecord.od.nih.gov/newsletters/2012/06_22_2012/story1.htm |title="Researchers, Advocates Gather to Accelerate Alzheimer's Research," ''NIH Record,'' June 22, 2012 |access-date=August 30, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130326154314/http://nihrecord.od.nih.gov/newsletters/2012/06_22_2012/story1.htm |archive-date=March 26, 2013 }}</ref> the [[Brain Research through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies]] (BRAIN) Initiative, announced by President Obama and Collins on April 2, 2013, at the White House; and in February 2014 the Accelerating Medicines Partnership (AMP), a public-private partnership between NIH, the [[Food and Drug Administration|U.S. Food and Drug Administration]], 10 biopharmaceutical firms, and multiple non-profit organizations.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Quinn |first1=Richard |title=Accelerating Medicines Partnership Advances Research for Autoimmune Diseases |url=https://www.the-rheumatologist.org/article/accelerating-medicines-partnership-advances-research-autoimmune-diseases/ |website=The Rheumatologist |publisher=American College of Rheumatology |access-date=1 January 2025 |date=November 11, 2016}}</ref>

In 2014, Collins worked with the larger biomedical research community to create principles and guidelines to foster rigor and reproducibility in preclinical research,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Collins|first1=Francis S.|last2=Tabak|first2=Lawrence A.|date=2014-01-30|title=Policy: NIH plans to enhance reproducibility|journal=Nature News|volume=505|issue=7485|pages=612–13|doi=10.1038/505612a|pmid=24482835|pmc=4058759|bibcode=2014Natur.505..612C}}</ref> including incorporating sex as a biological variable to ensure differences in treatment response between men and women are addressed.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Clayton|first1=Janine A.|last2=Collins|first2=Francis S.|date=2014-05-15|title=Policy: NIH to balance sex in cell and animal studies|journal=Nature News|volume=509|issue=7500|pages=282–283|doi=10.1038/509282a|pmid=24834516|pmc=5101948}}</ref>

Beginning in 2014, the NIH provided multi-year grants to [[EcoHealth Alliance]], which studied bat coronaviruses, including genetically engineering bat coronaviruses called [[Bat SARS-like coronavirus WIV1|WIV1]], in collaboration with the [[Wuhan Institute of Virology]].<ref name="Bat Research" /> The grants were terminated in 2020 under the Donald Trump administration, during Trump's feud with China over the origins of [[COVID-19]].<ref name="Bat Research" />{{relevance inline|date=July 2026}}<!--These two sentences make no mention of Collins, or how the head of the NOH might have been involved in these grants. If they were issued under a newly initiated program or funding line, Collins may have known or been involved. But study sections and program directors are involved in maaking decisions about grant funding (far below the NIH executive offices), and so citations and content must be offered to connect anything happening in such a large organisation to its head. Here, must make clear Collins' role, at the time, clear.-->

In January 2015, President Obama announced the NIH-led [[Precision Medicine Initiative]] (PMI), later renamed the All of Us Research Program, in his State of the Union address.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2015/01/30/fact-sheet-president-obama-s-precision-medicine-initiative|title=FACT SHEET: President Obama's Precision Medicine Initiative|date=January 30, 2015|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|access-date=April 29, 2016}}</ref> All of Us sought to extend precision medicine to all diseases by building a national research cohort of 1 million or more U.S. participants.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://allofus.nih.gov/ |title=Home |website=allofus.nih.gov}}{{full|date=July 2026}}</ref>{{full|date=July 2026}} In other precedent-setting actions during his time as NIH director, Collins announced in November 2015 that NIH will no longer support any biomedical research involving chimpanzees.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nih.gov/news/health/jun2013/od-26.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130630050812/http://www.nih.gov/news/health/jun2013/od-26.htm|archive-date=June 30, 2013|title=NIH to reduce significantly the use of chimpanzees in research|date=July 28, 2015|website=nih.gov|access-date=March 29, 2018}}</ref>

In December 2015, Collins and other NIH leaders released a detailed plan that charted a course for NIH's efforts over the ensuing five years. The NIH-Wide Strategic Plan, Fiscal Years 2016-2020: Turning Discovery Into Health was aimed at ensuring the agency remains well positioned to capitalize on new opportunities for scientific exploration and to address new challenges for human health.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nih.gov/about-nih/nih-wide-strategic-plan|title=NIH-Wide Strategic Plan|date=October 6, 2015|website=National Institutes of Health (NIH)|access-date=April 29, 2016}}</ref>

In January 2016, President Obama announced a new initiative to galvanize the nation's research efforts against cancer.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2016/02/01/fact-sheet-investing-national-cancer-moonshot|title=FACT SHEET: Investing in the National Cancer Moonshot|date=February 1, 2016|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|access-date=April 29, 2016}}</ref> Fueled by an additional $680 million in the proposed fiscal year 2017 budget for NIH, the National Cancer Moonshot Initiative aimed to accelerate progress toward the next generation of interventions to reduce cancer incidence and improve patient outcomes.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nih.gov/news-events/news-releases/blue-ribbon-panel-announced-help-guide-vice-president-bidens-national-cancer-moonshot-initiative|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160404192027/http://www.nih.gov/news-events/news-releases/blue-ribbon-panel-announced-help-guide-vice-president-bidens-national-cancer-moonshot-initiative|archive-date=April 4, 2016|title=Blue Ribbon Panel Announced to Help Guide Vice President Biden's National Cancer Moonshot Initiative|date=April 4, 2016|website=National Institutes of Health (NIH)|access-date=April 29, 2016}}</ref>{{relevance inline|date=July 2026}}<!--These two sentences make no mention of Collins, or how the White House decisions impacted his decisions or efforts.-->

In 2016, Collins instituted a number of clinical trial reforms<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Collins|first1=Francis S.|last2=Lauer|first2=Michael S.|last3=Hudson|first3=Kathy L.|date=2016-10-04|title=Toward a New Era of Trust and Transparency in Clinical Trials|journal=JAMA|volume=316|issue=13|pages=1353–1354|doi=10.1001/jama.2016.14668|pmid=27636028|issn=0098-7484|pmc=5101947}}</ref>  to enhance protection of participants in research and improve reporting of research results in ClinicalTrials.gov.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nih.gov/news-events/news-releases/hhs-takes-steps-provide-more-information-about-clinical-trials-public|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160916204640/https://www.nih.gov/news-events/news-releases/hhs-takes-steps-provide-more-information-about-clinical-trials-public|archive-date=September 16, 2016|title=HHS takes steps to provide more information about clinical trials to the public|date=2016-09-14|website=National Institutes of Health (NIH)|access-date=2019-07-30}}</ref> In 2017, Collins implemented the Next Generation Researchers Initiative<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://grants.nih.gov/policy-and-compliance/policy-topics/ngri|title=Next Generation Researchers Initiative {{!}} grants.nih.gov|website=grants.nih.gov|access-date=2019-07-30}}</ref> to improve the odds for early investigators to win NIH grants.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nih.gov/about-nih/who-we-are/nih-director/statements/launching-next-generation-researchers-initiative-strengthen-biomedical-research-enterprise|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170609205142/https://www.nih.gov/about-nih/who-we-are/nih-director/statements/launching-next-generation-researchers-initiative-strengthen-biomedical-research-enterprise|archive-date=June 9, 2017|title=Launching the Next Generation Researchers Initiative to Strengthen the Biomedical Research Enterprise|date=2017-06-08|website=National Institutes of Health (NIH)|access-date=2019-07-30}}</ref>

To support the Administration's Stop Opioid Abuse Initiative, Collins launched the NIH HEAL (Helping to End Addiction Long-term) Initiative in April 2018.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nih.gov/news-events/news-releases/nih-launches-heal-initiative-doubles-funding-accelerate-scientific-solutions-stem-national-opioid-epidemic|title=NIH launches HEAL Initiative, doubles funding to accelerate scientific solutions to stem national opioid epidemic|date=2018-04-03|website=National Institutes of Health (NIH)|access-date=2019-07-30}}</ref> The NIH HEAL Initiative bolstered research across NIH to improve treatments for opioid misuse and addiction and enhance pain management. Also in 2018, Collins launched an initiative to address sexual harassment in science and change a culture that sends messages to women and other underrepresented groups that they don't belong in biomedical research.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nih.gov/about-nih/who-we-are/nih-director/statements/changing-culture-science-end-sexual-harassment|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181023000912/https://www.nih.gov/about-nih/who-we-are/nih-director/statements/changing-culture-science-end-sexual-harassment|archive-date=October 23, 2018|title=Changing the culture of science to end sexual harassment|date=2018-09-17|website=National Institutes of Health (NIH)|access-date=2019-07-30}}</ref>

In October 2021, NIH principal deputy director [[Lawrence A. Tabak|Larry Tabak]] sent a letter to Kentucky Congressman [[James Comer]] addressing NIH grants to EcoHealth Alliance.<ref name="Bat Research"/> Comer, who has held hearings criticizing the use of U.S. federal funds for research related to bat coronaviruses in China, subsequently accused Collins of having potentially misled the [[United States House Committee on Oversight and Reform|Oversight Committee]] Republicans{{when|date=July 2026}} as to EcoHealth Alliance's activities.<ref name="Bat Research">{{cite news |last1=Zimmer |first1=Carl |last2=Mueller |first2=Benjamin |title=Bat Research Group Failed to Submit Virus Studies Promptly, N.I.H. Says |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/10/21/science/bats-covid-lab-leak-nih.html |work=The New York Times |date=21 October 2021}}</ref> 

In 2023, the [[Biden administration]] announced an initiative to eliminate [[hepatitis C]] in the United States.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-03-09 |title=White House makes push to eradicate hepatitis C |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/with-a-cure-available-for-hepatitis-c-white-house-aims-to-eradicate-the-disease |access-date=2024-07-28 |website=PBS News |language=en-us}}</ref> Collins was the special advisor to President Biden on the hepatitis C elimination plan.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Abbasi |first=Jennifer |date=2023-04-18 |title=Former NIH Director Francis S. Collins on the New White House Plan to Eliminate Hepatitis C |url=https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2802535 |journal=JAMA |language=en |volume=329 |issue=15 |pages=1246–1247 |doi=10.1001/jama.2023.3942 |pmid=36892977 |issn=0098-7484|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Collins's wrote an op-ed in The New York Times on the elimination plan advocating that the U.S. commit the appropriate resources.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Collins |first=Francis |date=2023-11-28 |title=We Are Squandering One of the Most Important Medical Advances of the 21st Century |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/11/28/opinion/hepatitis-c-eliminate.html |access-date=2024-07-28 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

== Acting science advisor ==
On February 17, 2022, President Biden named Collins the acting [[Science Advisor to the President|science advisor to the president]] after [[Eric Lander]] resigned.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Stolberg |first=Sheryl Gay |date=2022-02-17 |title=Francis Collins, a former N.I.H. director, will fill in as a science adviser to Biden. |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/02/17/us/politics/biden-francis-collins-nih.html |access-date=2022-03-22 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> He also serves as co-chair of the [[President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-02-16 |title=President Biden Announces OSTP Leadership |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/02/16/president-biden-announces-ostp-leadership/ |access-date=2022-03-22 |website=The White House |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Return to laboratory research and retirement==
After he stepped down as the director of NIH in December 2021, Collins returned to his 12-person research lab at NHGRI. Except for an eight-month stint as the acting presidential science advisor, Collins performed full-time biomedical research<ref>{{cite web |url=https://irp.nih.gov/pi/francis-collins |title=Francis Collins, M.D., Ph.D. |publisher=NIH |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250218094259/https://irp.nih.gov/pi/francis-collins |archive-date=2025-02-18 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.genome.gov/staff/Francis-S-Collins-MD-PhD |title=Francis Collins, M.D., Ph.D. |publisher=NHGRI |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250221185355/https://www.genome.gov/staff/Francis-S-Collins-MD-PhD |archive-date=2025-02-21 }}</ref> until he announced his retirement on February 28, 2025.<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/former-nih-director-francis-collins-retires-suddenly-makes-plea-protect-agency-staff |title='I won't miss the nasty politics.' Francis Collins reflects on his tenure at NIH |first=Jocelyn |last=Kaiser |date=December 20, 2021 |journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |doi=10.1126/science.z3uuccg|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Collins did not give a reason for his abrupt departure.<ref>{{cite news | author = Neergaard, Lauran | date = March 2, 2025 | via = The Associated Press | title=Renowned Geneticist Francis Collins Retires From NIH, Urging 'Respect' for Embattled Workers | newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]] | access-date = 2026-07-29 | url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2025/03/02/nation/francis-collins-retires-from-national-institute-of-health/ | url-access = subscription}}</ref>

In 2026, a book called 'Blockers'<ref>{{Cite web |last=The |first=Guardian |date=7 October 2026 |title=Blockers by Michael Lewis review – the quiet heroes who tried to stop Doge |url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/oct/07/blockers-by-michael-lewis-review-the-quiet-heroes-who-tried-to-stop-doge |url-status=live |website=The Guardian}}</ref> by Michael Lewis (author of books like 'Moneyball' and 'The Big Short') was published which described the campaign by the second Trump Administration to cut the civil service in its quest for 'efficiencies'. Francis Collins features in it and it alleges that he was 'forced out'. Lewis runs through a series of possible culprits, of which the cost-cutting is one. What makes this particularly ironic is that the Office of Management & Budget which implemented the cuts and most likely responsible for Collins' removal is run by Russell Vought, who has a daughter with cystic fibrosis.

==Music==
Collins's love of [[guitar]] playing and [[motor-cycle|motorcycle]] riding is often mentioned in articles about him.<ref>[http://www.slate.com/id/2222562 "Jesus Goes to Bethesda: Just how religious is Obama's nominee for director of the NIH?"]. Chris Wilson. ''[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]''. July 9, 2009</ref>

While directing NHGRI, he formed a [[Jazz|jazz band]] with other NIH scientists. Sometimes the band, called the Directors, dueled with a rock band from [[Johns Hopkins University]] led by cancer researcher [[Bert Vogelstein]]. Lyrics of the Directors' songs included spoofs of [[Rock music|rock]] and [[Gospel music|gospel]] classics re-written to address the challenges of contemporary biomedical research.<ref>*[http://www.nih.gov/catalyst/back/98.01/battle_of_bands.html "Science Writers Entertained By High-Powered Battle Of The Bands"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090703174657/http://www.nih.gov/catalyst/back/98.01/battle_of_bands.html |date=July 3, 2009 }}. ''The NIH Catalyst''. Celia Hooper. Jan/Feb 1998.</ref> Collins has performed at [[TEDMED]] 2012, StandUpToCancer,<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2010-sep-18-la-sci-francis-collins-jams-20100918-story.html |title=To scientists, he's the real rock star |last=Kaplan |first=Karen |date=September 18, 2010 |work=Los Angeles Times }}</ref> The 2017 [[Southern Methodist University]] Commencement<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.smu.edu/News/2017/Commencement-Francis-Collins-20may2017 |title=NIH Director Francis Collins addresses SMU students at 102nd Commencement |last=Kaplan |first=Karen |date=May 20, 2017 |access-date=June 4, 2017}}</ref> and Rock Stars of Science.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.geoffreybeene.com/pdf/RSOS_Program.pdf|title=Rock S.O.S. program, 2009|website=www.geoffreybeene.com|access-date=August 30, 2013|archive-date=May 21, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140521012139/http://www.geoffreybeene.com/pdf/RSOS_Program.pdf}}</ref>

His passion for [[music]] also inspired him to partner with the [[John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts|Kennedy Center]] to expand the Sound Health Initiative, which was announced in February 2017.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cms.kennedy-center.org/docs/default-source/public-relations-documents/2017-press-release-pdfs/02-february-2017/kcandnihpartnership.pdf|title=Sound Health Announcement}}</ref> Sound Health aims to expand current knowledge and explore ways to enhance the potential for music as therapy for [[Neurological disorder|neurological]] and other disorders.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nih.gov/research-training/medical-research-initiatives/sound-health|title=Sound Health|website=National Institutes of Health (NIH)|access-date=2019-07-30|archive-date=July 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190730124953/https://www.nih.gov/research-training/medical-research-initiatives/sound-health}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
While leading the [[National Human Genome Research Institute]], Collins was elected to the [[Institute of Medicine]] and the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]]. He was awarded the [[Canada Gairdner International Award]] in 1990. He was a [[Kilby International Awards]] recipient in 1993.<ref name="Nelson">{{cite web |last1=Nelson |first1=Richard William |title=The Extinction of "Junk DNA"  |date= September 18, 2012 |url=https://www.darwinthenandnow.com/2012/09/the-extinction-of-junk-dna/ |website=Then & Now |access-date=November 30, 2018}}</ref> Collins received the Golden Plate Award of the [[Academy of Achievement|American Academy of Achievement]] in 1994.<ref>{{cite web|title= Golden Plate Awardees of the American Academy of Achievement |website=www.achievement.org|publisher=[[American Academy of Achievement]]|url=https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#science-exploration}}</ref> He received the [[Association for Molecular Pathology]] Award for Excellence in Molecular Diagnostics in 1998.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Past Recipients |url=https://www.amp.org/membership/awards-grants-honors/amp-award-for-excellence-in-molecular-diagnostics/past-recipients/ |access-date=2023-03-03 |website=Association for Molecular Pathology |language=en}}</ref> He received the [[Biotechnology Heritage Award]] with [[J. Craig Venter]] in 2001, from the [[Biotechnology Industry Organization]] (BIO) and the [[Chemical Heritage Foundation]].<ref name="Biotechnology">{{cite web|title=Biotechnology Heritage Award|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/biotechnology-heritage-award|website=Science History Institute|date=May 31, 2016|access-date=March 22, 2018}}</ref><ref name=Strickland>{{cite news |last=Strickland |first=Debbie |title=Genomic Leaders Receive 2001 Biotechnology Heritage Award |url=http://www.bio.org/media/press-release/genomic-leaders-receive-2001-biotechnology-heritage-award |access-date=February 5, 2014 |publisher=BIO |date=June 13, 2001 |archive-date=January 9, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150109031918/https://www.bio.org/media/press-release/genomic-leaders-receive-2001-biotechnology-heritage-award }}</ref> Collins and Venter shared the "Biography of the Year" title from [[A&E Network]] in 2000.<ref>"[http://www.montgomerycountymd.gov/mc/news/press/00-463.html Montgomery County, Maryland, Press Releases] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061013151412/http://www.montgomerycountymd.gov/mc/news/press/00-463.html|date=October 13, 2006}}," December 19, 2000, URL accessed January 30, 2007.</ref> In 2005, Collins and Venter were honored as two of "America's Best Leaders" by ''[[U.S. News & World Report]]'' and the Harvard University [[Center for Public Leadership]].<ref>"[http://www.ksg.harvard.edu/leadership/usnews/genome.html U.S. News & World Report] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080123055322/http://www.ksg.harvard.edu/leadership/usnews/genome.html|date=January 23, 2008}}," 2005, URL accessed February 4, 2008.</ref>

In 2005 Collins received the [[William Allan Award]] from the [[American Society of Human Genetics]]. In 2007 he was presented with the [[Presidential Medal of Freedom]] by President George W. Bush.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://nihrecord.od.nih.gov/newsletters/2007/11_30_2007/story4.htm |title=NIH Record – ''Collins Wins Presidential Medal of Freedom'' |access-date=August 2, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100528170001/http://nihrecord.od.nih.gov/newsletters/2007/11_30_2007/story4.htm |archive-date=May 28, 2010 }}</ref> In 2008, he was awarded the Inamori Ethics Prize,<ref>[http://case.edu/events/inamori/prize/pastrecipients.html "Inamori Ethics Prize, Past Recipients," Case Western Reserve University] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120208115222/http://case.edu/events/inamori/prize/pastrecipients.html |date=February 8, 2012 }}</ref> as well as the [[National Medal of Science]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/od/nms/recip_details.cfm?recip_id=5300000000451|title=The President's National Medal of Science: Recipient Details - NSF - National Science Foundation|website=www.nsf.gov|access-date=March 29, 2018}}</ref> Also in 2008, Collins and [[Steven Weinberg]], a Nobel Prize recipient for physics, shared the [[Trotter Prize (Texas A&M)|Trotter Prize]], and discussed the interplay between science and religion.<ref>{{cite web|author=Nathan Ball|url=http://www.thebatt.com/2.8485/science-versus-religion-1.1187011|title=Science versus religion: Lecture series invitees discuss implications for scientific progress to support or suppress faith|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130203175330/http://www.thebatt.com/2.8485/science-versus-religion-1.1187011|archive-date=2013-02-03|date=March 25, 2008|magazine=The Battalion}}</ref> Collins received the [[Albany Medical Center Prize]] in 2010 and the Pro Bono Humanum Award of the Galien Foundation in 2012, the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology (FASEB) Public Service Award in 2017,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://faseb.org/Home.aspx|title=FASEB > Home|website=faseb.org|access-date=2019-07-30|archive-date=July 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190730124955/https://faseb.org/Home.aspx}}</ref> the Pontifical Key Scientific Award in 2018,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://vaticanconference2018.com/awards/2018-key-pontifical-key-scientific-award/|title=2018 Pontifical Key Scientific Award|last=jdyork|website=Global Health Care Initiative|access-date=2019-07-30}}</ref> and the Warren Alpert Foundation Prize in 2018.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://warrenalpert.org/prize-recipients|title=Prize Recipients|publisher=Warren Alpert Foundation Prize|access-date=2019-07-30}}</ref> In 2020, he received the [[Templeton Prize]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.templetonprize.org/francis-collins-awarded-2020-templeton-prize/|title=Francis Collins Awarded 2020 Templeton Prize|website=templetonprize.org|date=May 20, 2020|access-date=June 24, 2024}}</ref> and was elected a [[Foreign Member of the Royal Society]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/Francis-Collins-25416/|title=Francis Collins|publisher=Royal Society|access-date= 19 September 2020}}</ref> On October 2, 2025, Collins was awarded an honorary doctorate from [[Whitworth University]] in [[Spokane, Washington]], during an on-campus discussion titled, "The Road to Wisdom: On Truth, Science, Faith and Trust."<ref>{{Cite web |title=Renowned Geneticist and Former NIH Director Francis Collins to Headline Whitworth's Fall President's Leadership Forum on Oct. 2 |url=https://news.whitworth.edu/2025/06/renowned-geneticist-and-former-nih.html |access-date=2025-10-03}}</ref>  Collins was the 2026 [[Public Welfare Medal]] recipient from the National Academy of Sciences.<ref>{{Cite web |last=<!-- no byline --> |year=2026 |title=NAS Public Welfare Medal |url=https://www.nasonline.org/award/nas-public-welfare-medal/ |url-status=live |via=[[MSN]]}}</ref>

==Views==
===Christianity===
By graduate school, Collins considered himself [[agnostic]]. A conversation with a hospital patient led him to question his lack of religious views, and he investigated various faiths. He familiarized himself with the evidence for and against God in cosmology, and on the recommendation of a [[Methodist]] minister used ''[[Mere Christianity]]'' by [[C. S. Lewis]] as a foundation to develop his religious views. He believes that people cannot be converted to Christianity by reason and argument alone, and that the final stage of conversion entails a "[[leap of faith]]". After several years of deliberation, he finally converted to Christianity during a trip to the Cascade Mountains, where he describes a striking image of a frozen waterfall as removing his final resistance, resulting in his conversion the following morning.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.salon.com/2006/08/07/collins_6/|title=The believer|date=August 7, 2006 |work=[[Salon.com|Salon]] |first=Steve|last=Paulson|access-date=June 24, 2024}}</ref> He has described himself as a "serious Christian".<ref name=interview />

In his 2006 book ''[[The Language of God: A Scientist Presents Evidence for Belief]],'' Collins wrote that scientific discoveries were an "opportunity to worship" and that he rejected both [[Young Earth creationism]] and [[intelligent design]]. He wrote that his own belief was [[theistic evolution]] or [[evolutionary creation]], which he preferred to call [[BioLogos]]. He wrote that one can "think of DNA as an instructional script, a software program, sitting in the nucleus of the cell."<ref name="Collins2008">{{cite book |last=Collins |first=Francis |title=The Language of God: A Scientist Presents Evidence for Belief |date=September 4, 2008 |publisher=Simon and Schuster |isbn=978-1-84739-615-0}}</ref> He appeared on ''[[The Colbert Report]]'' and on ''[[Fresh Air]]'' radio to discuss his book.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cc.com/video-clips/dqyz7h/the-colbert-report-francis-collins |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161110064017/http://www.cc.com/video-clips/dqyz7h/the-colbert-report-francis-collins |archive-date=November 10, 2016 |title=Francis Collins |date=December 6, 2006 |access-date=March 15, 2020 |publisher=[[The Colbert Report]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite episode |title=Francis Collins on 'The Language of God{{'-}} |url=https://www.npr.org/2007/03/29/9207913/francis-collins-on-the-language-of-god |series=Fresh Air |series-link=Fresh Air |airdate=2007-03-29}}</ref> In an interview with [[D. J. Grothe]] on the ''[[Point of Inquiry]]'' podcast, he said that the overall aim of the book was to show that "one can be intellectually in a rigorous position and argue that science and faith can be compatible", and that he was prompted to write the book because "most people are seeking a possible harmony between these worldviews [science and faith], and it seems rather sad that we hear so little about this possibility."<ref name=languageofgod>{{cite web|url=http://www.pointofinquiry.org/dr_francis_collins_the_language_of_god/|title=''Dr. Francis Collins - The Language of God''|author=D.J. Grothe|publisher=[[Point of Inquiry]]|date=August 31, 2007|access-date=September 3, 2015|author-link=D.J. Grothe}}</ref> Collins said he had been a [[Methodism|Methodist]], [[Presbyterianism|Presbyterian]], [[Baptists|Baptist]], and [[Episcopalian]], emphasizing that denominational differences were not essential to him.<ref>{{cite interview |last=Collins |first=Francis S. |subject-mask=0 |interviewer-last=Abernethy |interviewer-first=Bob |interviewer-link=Bob Abernethy |title=Dr. Francis S. Collins Interview |url=https://www.pbs.org/wnet/religionandethics/2006/07/21/july-21-2006-dr-francis-s-collins-interview/3676/|date=2006-07-21 |work=[[Religion & Ethics Newsweekly]] |access-date=2026-07-25}}</ref> He recalled that, growing up, he participated in the choir of an [[Episcopal Church (United States)|Episcopal church]].<ref>{{cite interview |last=Collins |first=Francis S. |subject-mask=0 |title=Other Voices: Francis Collins|url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/questionofgod/voices/collins.html |work=The Question of God |publisher=[[PBS]] |year=2004 |access-date=2026-07-25}}</ref>

Collins is a critic of intelligent design, and for this reason he was not asked to participate in the 2008 documentary ''[[Expelled: No Intelligence Allowed]]''. Walt Ruloff, a producer for the film, stated that by rejecting intelligent design, Collins was "toeing the party line", a claim which Collins called "just ludicrous".<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/09/27/science/27expelled.html |work=The New York Times |title=Scientists Feel Miscast in Film on Life's Origin |first=Cornelia |last=Dean |date=September 27, 2007 |access-date=May 2, 2010}}</ref> In an interview he stated that "intelligent design is headed for collapse in the not too distant future" and that "science class ought to be about science, and opening the door to religious perspectives in that setting is a big mistake."<ref name=languageofgod/> In 2007, Collins founded the [[BioLogos Foundation]] to "contribute to the public voice that represents the harmony of science and faith." He served as the foundation's president until he was confirmed as director of the NIH.<ref>[http://biologos.org/news-events/francis-collins-confirmed-as-director-of-the-national-institutes-of-health/ BioLogos website] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090902103115/http://biologos.org/news-events/francis-collins-confirmed-as-director-of-the-national-institutes-of-health |date=September 2, 2009 }}</ref> Collins has also spoken at the [[Veritas Forum]] on the [[relationship between science and religion]] and the [[existence of God]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://veritas.org/speakers/francis-collins/|title=Francis Collins |work=[[Veritas Forum]] |archive-date=November 28, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151128042639/http://veritas.org/speakers/francis-collins}}</ref>

[[Christopher Hitchens]] referred to Collins as "one of the greatest living Americans", and stated that Collins was one of the most devout believers he had ever met.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hc6UdA3TtWY |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211221/hc6UdA3TtWY |archive-date=2021-12-21 |url-status=live|title=Christopher Hitchens says 'I'm dying.{{'-}}|last=ilisbaani|date=April 23, 2011|access-date=March 29, 2018|via=YouTube}}{{cbignore}}</ref> He further stated that Collins was sequencing the genome of the cancer that would ultimately claim Hitchens's life, and that their friendship despite their differing opinion on religion was an example of the greatest armed truce in modern times.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Wehner|first=Peter|date=2020-03-17|title=NIH Director: 'We're on an Exponential Curve{{'-}} |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2020/03/interview-francis-collins-nih/608221/|access-date=2021-04-13 |work=[[The Atlantic]]}}</ref>

===Agnosticism===

In an interview with ''National Geographic'' in February 2007, writer [[John Horgan (American journalist)|John Horgan]] criticized Collins's description of [[agnosticism]] as "a cop-out". In response, Collins clarified his position on agnosticism so as to exclude "earnest agnostics who have considered the evidence and still don't find an answer. I was reacting to the agnosticism I see in the scientific community, which has not been arrived at by a careful examination of the evidence. I went through a phase when I was a casual agnostic, and I am perhaps too quick to assume that others have no more depth than I did."<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20070203070802/http://www7.nationalgeographic.com/ngm/0702/voices.html Francis Collins: The Scientist as Believer] Feb. 2007</ref>

===Abortion===

In a 1998 interview with ''[[Scientific American]]'', Collins stated that he is "intensely uncomfortable with abortion as a solution to anything" and does not "perceive a precise moment at which life begins other than the moment of conception." In the same interview, it was said that Collins also "does not advocate changing the law".<ref>{{cite journal|year=1998|title=Profile: Where Science and Religion Meet|journal=[[Scientific American]]|volume=278|issue=2|pages=28–29|author=Beardsley T|doi=10.1038/scientificamerican0298-28|pmid=9490474}}</ref>
